rules.statement: Keep the stable internal principal id as the subject for every internal record and lookup (grants, consent, sessions, revocation, principal resolution), and apply a pairwise pseudonym only to the `sub` value emitted to a client.
rules.why: Grants, consent, sessions and revocation are cross-client joins keyed by the stable id. Putting the pseudonym in its place breaks those joins, such as 'revoke everything for this user'.
rules.check: Look for code that persists, keys or looks up grants, consent, sessions or revocation by a pairwise `sub`, or that writes the projected value back into the authenticated subject.

rules.statement: Derive a pairwise `sub` with a deterministic, stateless, one-way hash over the sector, principal id, tenant id and an optional secret salt. Join the inputs with a separator that cannot appear in any component, and don't persist a mapping from pseudonym to principal.
rules.why: A pure function always gives the same pseudonym for the same (sector, principal) pair without storage. A stored reverse map would keep exactly the link pairwise exists to hide, and an ambiguous join could let two different input sets produce the same hash.
rules.check: Look for pairwise derivations that use random or time-varying input, that concatenate inputs with no unambiguous separator, or that add a table, entity, store or migration mapping pseudonyms back to principals.

rules.statement: Never try to reverse a pairwise `sub` presented back to the server. Get the stable subject from server-side state (such as the session at end session), and refuse operations like token exchange whose only subject is a pairwise `sub` that doesn't resolve.
rules.why: The derivation is one-way and nothing is stored, so a pseudonym can't be resolved to a principal. Treating it as a principal id would be wrong or would need a forbidden reverse map.
rules.check: Look for code that resolves an inbound token's `sub` as a principal id without considering that it may be a pairwise pseudonym, or that tries to look up or invert pseudonyms.

rules.statement: Apply the subject projection at every place a client-facing `sub` is emitted (ID token, access token, back-channel `logout_token`, token introspection), and have UserInfo echo the access token's projected `sub` instead of computing its own.
rules.why: Every emitted `sub` must be pairwise so that relying parties and resource servers can't correlate users across sectors, and the UserInfo `sub` must equal the ID token's.
rules.check: Look for a new or changed issuance or response path that writes the raw principal id as `sub`, or that skips the projection service.

rules.statement: Resolve a pairwise sector as OpenID Connect Core §8.1 requires: use the host of `sector_identifier_uri` when it is set, otherwise the common host of the `redirect_uris`, otherwise fall back to the `client_id` rather than failing at issuance.
rules.why: The fallback treats a client with absent or ambiguous redirect hosts as its own sector, so it still gets a stable, non-correlatable `sub` instead of an error.
rules.check: Look at sector-resolution code for a wrong precedence order, or for throwing or returning an error when the redirect hosts are absent or ambiguous.

rules.statement: When a client registers a `sector_identifier_uri`, require an absolute `https` URI, fetch the document, require it to be a JSON array of strings, and verify that every registered redirect URI appears in it by ordinal match. Reject a failure with `invalid_client_metadata` on both create and update registration.
rules.why: Sector membership must be vouched for by whoever controls the document. Otherwise a client could claim another party's host as its sector and correlate or impersonate that sector's pseudonyms.
rules.check: Look for registration paths that accept a `sector_identifier_uri` without fetching and checking it, that allow non-https, that compare URIs case-insensitively or by prefix, or that validate on POST but not on PUT.

rules.statement: At registration, refuse a pairwise client whose `redirect_uris` span more than one host and that has no `sector_identifier_uri`.
rules.why: OpenID Connect Core §8.1 requires a `sector_identifier_uri` in this case, because otherwise the sector is ambiguous.
rules.check: Check that registration metadata validation rejects `subject_type=pairwise` with multi-host `redirect_uris` and no `sector_identifier_uri`.

rules.statement: Send every server-side fetch of a caller-supplied URL through the shared guarded outbound HTTP client. That client resolves the address and pins the connection away from private, loopback and link-local addresses, and it follows no redirects. Never make that block a setting that can be turned off.
rules.why: A fetch of a client-supplied URL is an SSRF sink that could reach cloud metadata or internal hosts. The private-address block is the non-negotiable floor.
rules.check: Look for `HttpClient` or `IHttpClientFactory` calls on URLs that come from callers or registrations and bypass the guarded client, for redirects being enabled, or for an option that disables the private-address block.

rules.statement: Don't guard against SSRF by checking only the URL's host string for private addresses. Resolve the address and pin the connection to the checked address.
rules.why: A hostname can resolve to a private address (DNS rebinding) and an IP literal can be obfuscated, so only a check that resolves and then pins is robust.
rules.check: Look for SSRF checks that parse `Uri.Host` or match IP strings without resolving the address and connecting to that same address.

rules.statement: Bound every fetch of a caller-supplied document with a timeout and a maximum response size, and read the body through a capped reader (such as `IOutboundHttpContentReader.ReadCappedAsync`) rather than buffering it without a limit.
rules.why: Untrusted callers can reach the fetch, so a slow or huge response must not tie up or exhaust the server.
rules.check: Look for outbound fetches of caller-supplied URLs that read the body with `ReadAsStringAsync` or `ReadAsByteArrayAsync`, or that have no timeout or size cap.

rules.statement: Keep extracting the stable subject from an inbound principal and projecting it to a client-facing pseudonym as two separate, distinctly named methods. Neither calls the other, and neither is treated as the other's inverse.
rules.why: The projection is one-way, so the two operations aren't inverses. Distinct names keep call sites unambiguous.
rules.check: Look for a projection method used where the stable subject should be extracted (or the reverse), for one method calling the other, or for a name suggesting they round-trip.
